Understood, and I am not arguing with April. My problem is the payment line. The unit price I can work with. Payment in advance is the only sticking point.
The advance is not greed, it is April again. And I already shaved two days off delivery at no charge, which nobody has thanked me for.

Every buyer asks me the same question, and it is always the wrong one. They ask why the price went up. The better question is when the price went up, because the answer is almost never this week. Take the line you are looking at now. We quoted it in February at a number we could hold until the end of March, and we said so in writing. If your purchase order had landed in March, you would have paid the February number, and none of us would be on this call. It did not land, the raw material moved eleven percent in April, and the quote in front of you is the honest version of that. Now, here is what I want you to hear. I am not telling you this to win the argument. I am telling you because there is a version of next year where this does not happen again. If we had had a rolling agreement in place, the April move would have been shared between us instead of landing entirely on you. So push me on the markup, by all means, and push me on the payment date. But if you only push on the number today, you will get four cents and the same phone call in twelve months.

The best deal I ever made is one I did not sign. Nine years ago I was buying a full line of equipment, and I had decided before the first call what my walk away number was. Not a wish, a number, written on the top of the page, with the reason next to it. On the third round we were six cents apart and in complete deadlock, and their director offered to split the difference. Three cents. Everyone in the room wanted me to take it. I said no, thank you, and I stood up, and I meant it. Two things happened. The first is that they called back eleven days later and met the number, which is the part people like to tell. The second is the part that actually matters. If I had taken the three cents that afternoon, I would have signed a contract with a payment schedule I had not read properly, because I was tired and it was late and the only thing left on my mind was the unit price. Walking away did not win me six cents. It bought me eleven days, and in those eleven days I found the clause that would have cost us a great deal more than six cents a unit, every month, for three years.

First, before the call, you write down the number where you walk away, with the reason next to it, so that a tired afternoon never decides it for you. Then, you open by asking for the reasoning behind the quote, and not by naming a figure of your own, because the first number on the table shapes everything after it. After that, you separate the sticking point from everything the two sides have already agreed, so that one open item does not quietly reopen the whole deal. Next, when neither side moves, you name the deadlock out loud and put a way out on the table, and splitting the difference is the cheapest one you have. Finally, you firm up the dates and the payment in writing the same day, while both sides still remember what they agreed and why.
